newsitem.title: USA: APRIL redemption paints bondholder losses.
newsitem.headline: APRIL redemption paints bondholder losses.

text.p: Holders of $300 million in debt from RAPP International Finance may sustain a $25 million loss if parent P.T. Riau Andalan Pulp and Paper proceeds with what it deems a mandatory redemption, sources in the corporate debt market said.

The redemption price in an indenture that would be triggered by sales of power and chemical assets by Riau Andalan Pulp and Paper (RAPP) has outraged holders of $100 11-1/2 percent and $200 million 13-1/4 percent bonds, currently valued at 105 and 111, respectively.

Riaupulp, also known as RAPP, last March proposed selling the power plant and chemical manufacturing assets that are part of its paper mill complex in Riau Province, Sumatra, Indonesia. Riaupulp Finance Director W. Michael Verge on Tuesday said Riaupulp "must complete (the sale) to stay competitive...and to finance future expansion."

Riaupulp is a 98.9 percent held operating subsidiary of the APRIL Group - Asia Pacific Resources International Holdings Ltd. APRIL Group officials said the expected asset sales would trigger an indenture to the bonds that mandates redemption of the debt at 101 percent of principal.
The indenture requires the redemption of the outstanding debt if certain assets are sold.
Riaupulp also has $250 in outstanding bank debt.
"Bondholders are getting screwed," said one analyst at a Wall Street investment bank who declined to be named. "If this goes through we're looking at a $25 million loss."
But analysts interviewed on Tuesday contend the sale is not so much a competitive move but merely an effort to escape high borrowing costs associated with the two 1995 debt offerings.

Some analysts questioned the company's intentions because the assets would be sold within the APRIL realm to Riau Prima Power and Indorayon. One analyst, who declined to be named, speculated the company could refinance the debt two to three percentage points lower on Asian debt markets.
The indenture requires that the move be made for legitimate business reasons, not for the purpose of redeeming the notes.
Neither Verge nor APRIL Finance Director Barry Kowock addressed questions about whether reduced interest payments are part of the expected savings.

Riaupulp in March said the sale was to provide funds to support expansion and reduce debt and operating costs. A statement made on Friday said most of the proceeds will be used to pay down indebtedness.

Officials said in the conference call Riaupulp would fall short of the $550 million paydown by $140 million. That shortfall would be made up with $40 million in land sales and a $100 million advance from APRIL Group.

Analysts said a bondholder waiver of the indenture was not in the offing. Riaupulp's finance director, Verge, told noteholders they had no right to opt out of the redemption and Riaupulp has no intention to offer them a chance to do so. But one analyst questioned Verge's reading of the situation.
"That's not necessarily the whole truth," the analyst said. "You can always amend the indenture."
The redemption is contingent on fairness opinions from Merrill Lynch & Co for the power assets and from SBC Warburg for the chemical assets.

Corinne Moloff, vice president and analyst at Alliance Capital Management, said the Riaupulp's move will likely cast a pall over other outstanding Indonesian corporate debt and any new issuance. Alliance does not hold RAPP paper, she said.
"This does not bode well for other Indonesian issuers," Moloff said. "They are really doing a disservice to other issuers that have to come to market because there will now be a certain skepticism."

Steven Gallen Edersheim, director of international fixed-income at Schroder Wertheim & Co, said a snub of Indonesian credits would be misguided. The situation is a result of questionable covenants, he said, and that has occurred in many other markets and industries.
"This is another instance of a recurring problem in the corporate bond market," Edersheim said. "There is an inherent conflict of interest between the bondholders and the shareholders."
--U.S. corporate bonds, 212-859-1672
